newsitem.title: UK: World oil price slide, continuing week of losses.
newsitem.headline: World oil price slide, continuing week of losses.

text.p: World oil prices reversed slight early gains, falling sharply on Friday, the fourth day of decline this week. The benchmark Brent blend on London's International Petroleum Exchange broke through the psychological support level of $18, settling a hefty 62 cents lower at $17.70 a barrel.
In New York, crude oil futures plunged to a 15-month low as the market failed to stop a three-day decline .

In early trading, the London futures rose to a high of $18.51, with the market taking some comfort from perdictions of faster demand growth next year. But New York's fall, prompted the slide in London.

Oil prices have fallen steadily since Tuesday after institutional futures buyers were frightened into a hefty sell-off by bearish supply fundamentals such as the renewal of the United Nations deal allowing Iraq to export oil in exchange for food and medicines.

Although a report from the International Energy Agency (IEA) was described as mildly supportive, Friday's early bounce upwards was mostly ascribed to technical pricing factors and few market professionals expected values to recover much ground.
Crude sellers have been looking to the North American gasoline market to buoy demand.

However, frantic production at U.S. refineries has more than adequately supplied the increased summer demand for motor fuel, and unleaded gasoline futures hit an unseasonal 10-month low in New York on Thursday.

The IEA, the West's oil watchdog, forecast that oil demand would grow at a faster rate next year than in 1997, spurred on by the appetite of developing countries and stronger economies in the former Soviet Union.
The Paris-based IEA's monthly reports said world oil demand should grow by 1.85 million barrels per day (bpd) to 75.5 million bpd in 1998.

It also revised upwards its estimated fourth quarter demand for oil from OPEC members to make up for shortfalls in production in non-OPEC countries, which have been hit by delays in bringing new fields on stream.
"The report was not as bearish as some people were expecting," said one broker.
However the IEA's good news was tempered by predictions of soaring supply.
"The world oil market in 1998 is expected to be well-supplied, as growth in non-OPEC oil production is expected to exceed the growth in world oil demand," the IEA said.
Analysts also doubted that the increased demand for Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries oil would cut deep into the 11-nation cartel's over-production.

"Even after these revisions the numbers are extremely bearish. (IEA forecast) demand (in 1998) for OPEC at 25.3 million bpd is still two million bpd adrift of current output," said Geoff Pyne, oil analyst at UBS in London.
OPEC output in May stood at 26.95 million bpd, well above the official production ceiling of 25.03 million bpd, according to a Reuters survey.
Maintenance at OPEC fields hit May production, helping prices to firm, but the outlook was gloomy for later in the year when wells should be pumping at full strength, analysts said.
